blocks.heading: Users need different financial evidence
blocks.text: Managers use accounts for planning, control and decisions about resources. Owners and potential investors assess returns, risk and how their investment is used. Lenders assess repayment prospects and financial strength; suppliers offering credit assess whether short-term debts are likely to be paid. Employees may assess job security and the ability to sustain pay, while government may use appropriate records for public revenue and policy purposes. Customers with a long-term supply arrangement may assess continuity of supply. Users may emphasise different figures: a shareholder may focus on return, whereas a short-term supplier needs cash timing and liquidity as well. Financial statements are historical, summarised and affected by valuation; they do not capture every service-quality or management factor. Ratios are evidence for a decision, not a substitute for checking the user’s actual concern.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri Traders: annual turnover N$240,000, cost of sales N$144,000, other expenses N$72,000, credit sales N$219,000 and credit purchases N$146,000. At year end: non-current assets N$90,000; inventory N$30,000; debtors N$18,000; cash N$12,000; current liabilities N$30,000 (including creditors N$20,000); non-current liabilities N$40,000; owner’s equity N$80,000. Opening inventory was N$18,000. Use the opening and closing inventory average for inventory turnover. No other income or expense is assumed in this simple example. A supplier considering short credit for Neri should examine current and quick ratios, debtor collection and near-term payments. An owner considering returns would also examine the 20.00% ROCE and profit margins. The supplier cannot conclude that a profitable business must pay on time, and the owner cannot judge the full return from the current ratio alone.
